vignette:
Liam Rourke, a 32-year-old combat pilot, came to treatment after months of telling himself that what was happening to him was proof that he was failing at something other people would handle. The assault had occurred during a deployment, after a night when he had been drinking with another service member he knew well and had trusted. What stayed with him was not only the physical violation but the moment he understood, too late, that the man in front of him was not safe. He still fixated on small details from that night: the shift in the other man’s tone, the sense that the situation had turned without warning, the feeling of being trapped in an encounter he had not seen coming. That betrayal became the meaning he carried forward. He had come to believe that if someone he trusted could do this, then people were fundamentally unsafe and the world could turn dangerous without notice.

In the weeks afterward, Liam found that certain moments hit him with an intensity that seemed to come out of nowhere but made complete sense to him once he felt it in his body. Men behaving in ways he read as suspicious—lingering too close, watching him too carefully, changing their manner suddenly—immediately raised his guard. Unpredictable situations were especially hard; if plans changed suddenly, if someone approached him unexpectedly, if he could not tell what another person intended, his body reacted before he could reason with it. The worst mornings were after nightmares. He would wake abruptly with the residue of the dream still clinging to him, disoriented and already tense, as if the day had begun in the middle of danger. Because he had come to see betrayal and sudden threat as built into other people and into life itself, these moments did not feel like overreactions to him; they felt like accurate warnings.

Those warnings quickly organized his daily life around watchfulness. At home, Liam listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering his apartment. A creak in the hallway, a neighbor at the wrong door, the click of the building’s front entrance could make him jolt upright. He startled at ordinary sounds that he knew should not bother him—an ice maker dropping cubes, a phone vibrating against the counter, footsteps overhead—yet his body reacted as if an intrusion were underway. Even inside his own home he did not feel off duty. Waking from a nightmare made this worse; on those mornings he would move through the apartment checking locks and scanning rooms, already on guard. In public, people he deemed suspicious and any situation that felt unpredictable drew the same tense, listening attention, as though his safety depended on catching danger a second before it arrived.

Over time, Liam’s interpretations of himself hardened around these reactions. Each time he jumped at a noise in his apartment or spent the night listening for someone entering, he took it as evidence that he was, in his words, “a lousy coper.” As a combat pilot, he was used to valuing steadiness under pressure, rapid assessment, and control. Being unable to relax in his own home felt humiliating to him. The more on edge he felt, the more convinced he became that something in him had been damaged by the assault and that he could no longer trust his own resilience. That belief did not stay abstract; it sharpened his scanning. If he was this shaken, he reasoned, then he had better stay alert, because clearly he could not count on himself to handle being caught off guard again.

His work environment gave these patterns constant opportunities to tighten. On base and around the airfield, unpredictability is built into the day—schedule changes, sudden directives, people entering shared spaces without warning—and Liam found himself reacting to those moments with the same internal jolt he felt elsewhere. A crew member appearing behind him unexpectedly or a shift in plans could leave him keyed up long afterward. When another person’s manner struck him as off, he found himself studying tone and posture for signs of danger. The more he lived this way, the less faith he had in people, and that loss of faith made suspicious behavior stand out even more quickly. Then his body would surge into alertness again, confirming to him that he was right not to trust.

By the time he sought help, Liam was exhausted by the sense that he could never fully stand down. He was still single, and part of that felt safer to him now; closeness had become tangled with risk. What finally pushed him into treatment was not one dramatic incident but the accumulation of mornings spent waking from nightmares already braced, evenings spent listening for someone entering his home, and the growing conviction that these reactions meant he was becoming someone weaker and smaller than he had been before. He came in wanting relief, but also afraid that if he stopped watching, he would be betrayed again—and afraid, too, that if nothing changed, this guarded, mistrustful version of himself was all that would be left.
